paragraphs: A market maker needs a trading strategy that can cope with changing asset prices. Guarantees about profit often depend on specific probabilistic assumptions about how those prices fluctuate. This paper develops a class of strategies based on trading spreads whose performance can instead be controlled in a worst-case setting, where price movements may be adversarial.

The authors prove structural properties of this strategy class and use them to build a master algorithm. Its guarantee concerns regret: how much performance it loses relative to the best strategy from that class, chosen after seeing the price sequence. This provides a way to adapt across available strategies while retaining a meaningful retrospective comparison.

Experiments on real price data show favorable performance. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: whether adaptation can be controlled under adverse price sequences, and whether the approach works favorably on observed data. The guarantee is relative to the specified strategy class; it does not establish unconditional profitability.
neurips-2013-adaptive-market-making-via-.tldr: An online market-making algorithm achieves low regret against a class of spread-based strategies, with favorable results on real price data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to draw samples from distributions over binary variables. Such variables have discrete alternatives, while Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a method built around movement through a continuous representation. The central idea is to augment the binary distribution with auxiliary variables so that an exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm can be applied to a piecewise continuous representation.

The augmentation supplies the connection between the binary sampling problem and the continuous algorithm. The authors also extend the approach to distributions containing both binary and continuous variables. This makes the framework applicable to posterior sampling in linear and probit regression with spike-and-slab priors and truncated parameters, combining discrete choices with continuous quantities.

Several examples illustrate advantages over Metropolis or Gibbs sampling. These comparisons support the usefulness of the proposed samplers in the examples studied. The broader methodological contribution is a construction that makes exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo available for binary distributions and extends the same idea to mixed-variable inference problems.
neurips-2013-auxiliary-variable-exact-ha.tldr: Auxiliary variables enable exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling for binary and mixed-variable distributions, outperforming Metropolis or Gibbs samplers in several examples.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. This paper introduces B-tests, a family of kernel tests based on maximum mean discrepancy. Their purpose is to combine efficient use of data with manageable computation, rather than requiring a quadratic number of kernel evaluations to obtain useful statistical estimates.

A tunable parameter controls the tradeoff between computational time and sample requirements. The tests use the available observations to obtain low-variance estimates in finite samples, while avoiding the complicated null-hypothesis approximation required by the comparison approach based on one-sample U-statistics. This connects the statistical design directly to the cost of carrying out the test.

The authors establish consistency and probabilistically conservative thresholds for Type I error, the error of rejecting a true same-distribution hypothesis. Existing methods for combining multiple kernels also carry over to B-tests, potentially improving discrimination and reducing sample requirements further. The contribution is therefore both a testing family and a flexible computation-versus-data tradeoff.
neurips-2013-b-test-a-non-parametric-low.tldr: B-tests offer consistent kernel two-sample testing with tunable computational cost, low-variance estimates, and conservative Type I error thresholds.

paragraphs: This paper studies how people search for the maximum of an unknown function. Participants click locations on a blank screen and see the function value at each selected location. Their goal is to get sufficiently close to the maximum using as few clicks as possible. The task exposes both the quality of their decisions and the sequence of locations they investigate.

In a study involving 23 non-mathematics undergraduates and 25 functions from different families, humans outperform 24 established optimization algorithms. Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization better predicts human performance and search locations. It selects new locations using all previously observed inputs and function values, providing a computational account of how accumulated evidence can guide search.

Six additional controlled experiments involving 76 participants examine interpolation, extrapolation, and optimization. Together, the findings support Gaussian processes as a unified theoretical account of passive and active function learning in these tasks. The contribution links a model of learning unknown functions to observed human choices, beyond simply comparing final search success.
neurips-2013-bayesian-optimization-expla.tldr: Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization explains human search choices and performance across experiments involving unknown functions.

paragraphs: A Markov chain's stationary distribution describes its long-run allocation of probability across states. Computing it can be expensive when the state space is large or countably infinite. Standard approaches may repeatedly operate across the state space or simulate long random walks. This paper asks a more targeted question: does one selected state have stationary probability above a chosen threshold?

The proposed algorithm answers that threshold question and, when the probability is above the threshold, estimates its value. It uses information from a local neighborhood in the graph defined by the Markov chain. The neighborhood has constant size relative to the overall state space, allowing the procedure to focus on the state of interest.

Correctness and convergence guarantees depend on algorithm settings and the chain's mixing properties, which describe how it approaches stationary behavior. Simulations exhibit chains for which the estimates are tight. The result shows how a local probability query can avoid the work of computing an entire stationary distribution, subject to those dependencies.
neurips-2013-computing-the-stationary-di.tldr: A local algorithm tests whether a selected Markov-chain state exceeds a stationary-probability threshold and estimates that probability when it does.

paragraphs: A learning system may be judged by a target loss that is difficult to optimize directly. A surrogate loss provides an alternative training objective. The key theoretical question is whether optimizing that alternative is aligned with the original goal. This paper constructs convex surrogates that are calibrated, meaning their minimization supports consistency with respect to the desired target loss.

The construction applies to multiclass problems whose target loss matrix has low rank. That matrix records the costs associated with predictions and outcomes; its rank captures structure that can reduce the dimension needed for the surrogate. The proposed least-squares-style loss uses a target space with dimension no greater than the matrix rank.

The authors apply the construction to subset ranking, covering precision at a specified cutoff, expected rank utility, mean average precision, and pairwise disagreement. These applications show how one structural result can produce calibrated objectives for several distinct evaluation criteria. The contribution is an explicit design method connecting convex optimization, dimensionality, and the loss that ultimately matters.
neurips-2013-convex-calibrated-surrogate.tldr: Low-rank loss matrices enable explicit convex, calibrated surrogates whose dimension is at most the target loss matrix's rank.

paragraphs: Classes with few training examples can benefit from information learned about related classes. This paper represents those relationships through a tree hierarchy. The tree supplies a generative prior over classification parameters, creating a structured way for related classes to share knowledge while retaining a discriminative model for the classification task.

The authors show how these priors can be combined with models such as deep neural networks. They also introduce an algorithm for learning the tree itself. This allows the relationships used for transfer to adapt to the task, rather than depending entirely on a fixed semantic hierarchy chosen in advance.

The method transfers knowledge across related classes using fixed semantic trees and can learn meaningful new trees, usually improving performance. The paper reports state-of-the-art classification results on CIFAR-100 and the MIR Flickr multimodal dataset. Its central contribution is the combination of discriminative training with structured parameter sharing, including the ability to learn which class relationships are useful.
neurips-2013-discriminative-transfer-lea.tldr: Tree-based priors let discriminative classifiers share knowledge across related classes, improving learning when examples are scarce.

paragraphs: The Skip-gram model learns word vectors that capture grammatical and semantic relationships. This paper improves how quickly it learns and the quality of its representations. One change is to subsample frequent words, reducing their presence during training. On the authors' evaluation tasks, this both substantially speeds up learning and produces better vectors.

The paper also introduces Negative Sampling, a simplified form of Noise Contrastive Estimation. Compared with hierarchical softmax, it learns more accurate representations for frequent words. This is a specific comparison about representation quality for that group of words, alongside the broader aim of making Skip-gram training more efficient and expressive.

A further contribution addresses phrases whose meanings cannot readily be assembled from their individual words. The authors introduce a simple, efficient phrase-discovery method and show that Skip-gram can accurately learn vectors for the resulting phrases. This extends the units represented by the model, allowing an idiomatic phrase to have its own representation instead of relying only on separate word vectors.
neurips-2013-distributed-representations.tldr: Frequent-word subsampling, Negative Sampling, and phrase discovery improve the speed, quality, and expressiveness of Skip-gram representations.

paragraphs: In sequential decision-making, selecting an action can reveal information about other actions as well as the chosen one. An observability graph describes these feedback relationships. This paper studies the resulting partial-observation problem, connecting the amount and structure of available feedback to regret, a measure of accumulated performance relative to a comparison strategy.

For directed observability graphs, where feedback relationships need not be reciprocal, the main result characterizes regret through the graph's domination and independence numbers. These quantities capture different aspects of how actions provide information about one another. The result makes the arrangement of feedback relationships central to understanding the difficulty of learning.

For undirected graphs, the authors show that optimal regret is achievable even without accessing the observability graph before choosing an action. Both results use computationally efficient variants of Exp3 that operate on these graphs. The work therefore connects structural performance guarantees with implementable algorithms, while establishing that advance graph access is unnecessary for the stated undirected result.
neurips-2013-from-bandits-to-experts-a-t.tldr: Observability-graph structure characterizes regret in partial-feedback learning, with optimal regret achievable without advance graph access in the undirected case.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether models trained for object recognition can develop representations resembling those in the brain's ventral visual stream. The comparison uses representation dissimilarity matrices, which record distances among responses to visual stimuli. Those responses can come from model features, neural firing rates, or fMRI measurements, allowing their patterns of similarity to be compared.

The authors construct models using a new optimization procedure for category-level object recognition. Their models produce dissimilarity matrices resembling those measured in macaque inferotemporal cortex and the human ventral stream. This addresses a gap identified in prior work, where existing models failed to capture the observed patterns of representational distances.

The finding concerns how visual stimuli are organized within the representations, providing a connection between a recognition objective and brain measurements. It develops the hypothesis that the ventral stream consists of hierarchical processing stages optimized for recognizing objects. The reported resemblance supports that functional account through representational comparison, rather than establishing identity between the model and biological processing.
neurips-2013-hierarchical-modular-optimi.tldr: A new object-recognition optimization procedure produces model representations resembling those in macaque IT cortex and the human ventral stream.

paragraphs: Clustering groups observations without supplied class labels, but the information useful for grouping may not be directly observed. This paper introduces a maximum-margin clustering framework with latent variables. These hidden representations let the method account for information embedded in the data while learning a separation between the resulting groups.

The authors formulate the framework through large-margin learning and develop an alternating descent algorithm for its non-convex optimization problem. They instantiate the approach for tag-based video clustering. Each video receives a latent tag representation describing whether tags are present or absent, making hidden tag information part of the representation used to cluster videos.

Experiments on three standard datasets show better results than non-latent maximum-margin clustering and conventional clustering methods. These findings support the usefulness of latent representations in the evaluated video tasks. The methodological contribution is to combine learning hidden information with margin-based grouping, rather than requiring the clustering procedure to work only with a representation that has already been fixed.
neurips-2013-latent-maximum-margin-clust.tldr: Latent maximum-margin clustering learns hidden representations and improves tag-based video clustering on three evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Learning several models from one dataset includes problems such as clustering, multiple regression, and subspace clustering. Common approaches extend Lloyd's algorithm or expectation-maximization. The paper identifies a robustness problem with this pattern: under outliers or substantial noise, a single exceptional observation can effectively capture one of the models.

The proposed formulation assigns each model a distribution of weights over observations. Regularization requires those weights to remain sufficiently spread out, reducing the ability of one observation to dominate a model. This robustness relies on assumptions about class balance, making the distribution of data across groups part of the method's statistical foundation.

The authors provide generalization bounds and explain how to compute the resulting iterations efficiently. Experiments demonstrate robustness benefits, and a clustering-specific result establishes a nonzero breakdown point: the method tolerates a fixed percentage of adversarial outliers even when their values are unbounded. The framework thus combines a general modeling formulation with a concrete robustness guarantee for clustering.
neurips-2013-learning-multiple-models-vi.tldr: Regularizing each model's weights across observations improves robustness, with a provable nonzero breakdown point for clustering under class-balance assumptions.

paragraphs: A seller offering prices repeatedly must learn about a buyer's value for a good. This becomes more complicated when the buyer acts strategically to maximize surplus over the whole interaction. Motivated by online advertising exchanges, the paper studies posted-price mechanisms in which the seller seeks long-term revenue while learning the buyer's value distribution.

The authors present seller algorithms with no-regret guarantees when the buyer discounts future surplus. Discounting means the buyer values an earlier benefit more than the same benefit received later. In the advertising interpretation, the buyer prefers showing advertisements sooner. This preference is a substantive condition enabling the seller's learning guarantee.

A lower bound shows that regret becomes harder to control as the buyer's discounting weakens. With no discounting, every seller algorithm suffers linear regret in the studied setting. Together, these results identify buyer patience as a central determinant of what the seller can learn and earn, rather than treating purchase decisions as passive observations.
neurips-2013-learning-prices-for-repeate.tldr: Seller algorithms achieve no regret against a strategic buyer who discounts future surplus, while no discounting makes linear regret unavoidable.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning from the teacher's perspective. A teacher knows the intended learning goal and can design training examples for a Bayesian learner. The question is which examples to provide when both the learner's eventual errors and the effort required to teach matter. The authors express this tradeoff as an optimization problem over teaching data.

The general optimization problem is difficult. For learners using conjugate exponential-family models, the paper develops an approximate algorithm that first works with aggregate sufficient statistics. These statistics summarize the information from examples that is relevant to the model. Optimizing the summary provides an intermediate representation of the teaching set.

The algorithm then unpacks the optimized statistics into actual examples that can be shown to the learner. Several examples illustrate the framework. Its contribution is a concrete way to connect a desired learning outcome to deliberately constructed training data, while accounting for teaching effort. The approximate solution applies to the specified model family rather than solving the general teaching problem exactly.
neurips-2013-machine-teaching-for-bayesi.tldr: An optimal-teaching framework balances Bayesian learner error and teaching effort, with an approximate algorithm based on sufficient statistics for conjugate exponential-family models.

paragraphs: In high-dimensional regression, there are more candidate covariates than observations. This paper assumes that only a small subset truly has nonzero coefficients and asks how to identify it. The goal is model selection: recovering the active variables, rather than merely obtaining predictions from a fitted regression.

Lasso is a common approach, but identifying the active set requires an irrepresentability condition restricting the relationship between relevant and irrelevant covariates. The paper studies the Gauss-Lasso selector, which first fits Lasso and then performs ordinary least squares using the variables selected by Lasso. This creates a two-stage route to identifying the active set.

The authors formulate a generalized irrepresentability condition that is substantially weaker than the original condition. Under this assumption, they prove that Gauss-Lasso correctly recovers the active variables. The result expands the conditions under which recovery can be guaranteed for the two-stage method. Its force comes from weakening a structural assumption while retaining a model-selection guarantee, with that guarantee still conditional on the generalized requirement.
neurips-2013-model-selection-for-high-di.tldr: Gauss-Lasso recovers active regression variables under a generalized irrepresentability condition that is substantially weaker than the usual one.

paragraphs: A set of k-means centers can fit a finite dataset well without immediately revealing how well it fits the distribution that produced the data. This paper bounds the gap between those two costs when the source distribution has bounded moments of order p, with p at least four. The question applies even when the centers were obtained through heuristic optimization.

For m observations, the stated dependence of the gap is m raised to min{-1/4, -1/2 + 2/p}. The central technical contribution is a mechanism for controlling deviations uniformly despite unbounded parameter sets, costs, and source distributions. This matters because the analysis must cover the fitted choice of centers, not just one choice fixed beforehand.

The authors also apply the mechanism to Gaussian-mixture log likelihood, viewed as a soft-clustering counterpart, under a bounded-spectrum condition on covariance matrices. They provide refined constants for k-means problems with cluster structure. Together, these results connect finite-sample clustering quality to distribution-level fit under explicit moment and structural conditions.
neurips-2013-moment-based-uniform-deviat.tldr: Moment-based uniform bounds relate observed k-means cost to population cost and extend to constrained Gaussian-mixture clustering.

paragraphs: Some time series contain a multidimensional array at every time step. These arrays, called tensors, have a structure that is lost when each observation is treated simply as a vector. This paper introduces multilinear dynamical systems to extract hidden, changing trends while preserving the tensor form of the observations.

The model represents each observed tensor as a multilinear projection of a corresponding low-dimensional latent tensor. A sequence of these hidden tensors describes the evolving underlying representation. The authors also develop an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate the model's parameters, giving a fitting procedure alongside the new model.

On both simulated and real datasets, the method achieves higher prediction accuracy and marginal likelihood than a linear dynamical system with the same number of parameters. Matching parameter counts makes the comparison informative about the value of the tensor-based structure. The stated results support modeling multidimensional observations directly when extracting temporal trends, rather than assuming that a vector representation uses the modeling capacity equally well.
neurips-2013-multilinear-dynamical-syste.tldr: Multilinear dynamical systems preserve tensor structure and outperform equally parameterized linear dynamical systems on the evaluated time-series datasets.

paragraphs: Online decisions become harder when losses respond to the learner's behavior. This paper studies adaptive adversaries in prediction with expert advice under full-information and bandit feedback. It evaluates performance using policy regret, a notion intended to account for that adaptiveness, and considers a setting where losses may drift over time.

With switching costs, the attainable bandit-feedback rate is T to the two-thirds power, where T is the time horizon. Under full information, the corresponding attainable rate is the square root of T. The comparison shows that observing less feedback changes the achievable rate substantially when moving between actions incurs a cost.

The authors further show that an adversary with bounded memory can force T to the two-thirds regret even under full information. A reduction from experts to bandits establishes this separation, showing that switching costs are easier to control than general bounded-memory adaptation. Their lower bounds use a stochastic adversary that creates strongly dependent losses, helping characterize the difficulty of these adaptive settings.
neurips-2013-online-learning-with-switch.tldr: Policy-regret bounds distinguish the difficulty of switching costs, limited feedback, and bounded-memory adversaries in online learning.

paragraphs: Online principal component analysis estimates important directions in data as samples arrive sequentially. Outliers can make previous online PCA estimates arbitrarily poor. This paper develops an online robust PCA algorithm designed to improve an initial estimate steadily even when a constant fraction of the incoming observations are outliers.

The authors show that the final estimate has a controlled degradation from the optimum. Under mild conditions, the method attains a 50% breakdown point, described as maximal robustness. A breakdown point concerns how much contamination an estimator can withstand before its behavior can become arbitrarily bad, so the stated conditions matter to interpreting this robustness claim.

The algorithm also avoids revisiting earlier observations, unlike traditional robust PCA methods that re-explore previous samples. This supports efficiency in both storage and computation and makes the approach suitable for large datasets. The contribution combines resistance to contamination with sequential processing: it aims to improve principal-component estimates without repeatedly processing the full history of data.
neurips-2013-online-pca-for-contaminated.tldr: Online robust PCA improves estimates despite outliers, avoids revisiting past samples, and reaches a 50% breakdown point under mild conditions.

paragraphs: An instructional policy specifies what learners encounter and how instruction unfolds. For concept learning, it might determine how example difficulty changes over a training sequence. Traditional experiments compare a few policies selected by researchers. This paper instead defines a parameterized policy space and searches it for the policy that produces the best learning outcomes.

The proposed experimental method combines Gaussian-process surrogate optimization with a generative model of student performance. It evaluates many conditions using relatively few participants in each, rather than concentrating many participants into a small number of conditions. The optimization procedure uses noisy individual outcomes to infer the shape of the policy space and identify its global optimum.

The authors evaluate the method in two behavioral studies and report efficiency in participant use comparable to a traditional A-B comparison. This matters because the same experimental budget can support a broader search over instructional choices. They also suggest applicability to human-centered optimization beyond education, extending the methodological idea of searching policies through noisy behavioral measurements.
neurips-2013-optimizing-instructional-po.tldr: Gaussian-process optimization searches instructional policy spaces using noisy student outcomes with participant-budget efficiency comparable to an A-B comparison.

paragraphs: Graph kernels provide a way to compare graphs, including graphs whose nodes carry continuous-valued attributes. Existing methods for this setting can be computationally expensive. The paper highlights the shortest-path kernel, whose runtime scales as the fourth power of the number of nodes, as an example of the difficulty in handling larger graphs.

The authors introduce a class of path kernels with complexity O(n²(m + δ²)), where n is the number of nodes, m the number of edges, and δ the graph diameter. This expression makes the edge count and diameter central to computational cost. Sparse graphs with small diameter are favorable cases, motivating the approach for real-world graph data.

In classification benchmark experiments, the proposed kernels outperform the compared state-of-the-art methods in both speed and accuracy. The results therefore address predictive usefulness as well as computational scaling. The contribution is a path-based way to compare continuously attributed graphs whose efficiency benefits from graph structure, with empirical support on the evaluated classification tasks.
neurips-2013-scalable-kernels-for-graphs.tldr: New path kernels compare graphs with continuous node attributes efficiently and improve speed and accuracy on evaluated classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models describe sequences using unobserved states, but inference can be computationally demanding. This paper uses small-variance asymptotics to derive simpler combinatorial algorithms from these probabilistic models. The approach studies what happens as particular model variances tend to zero, translating a probabilistic formulation into a hard-assignment inference problem.

For the standard hidden Markov model, the resulting algorithm resembles k-means. The authors extend the analysis to an infinite-state Bayesian nonparametric model, producing an algorithm whose number of states is not fixed in advance. They also derive explicit objectives containing a k-means-like fit term and penalties involving state transitions and the number of states.

These objectives preserve sequence-related structure while providing a simple and scalable computational approach. The motivation is especially relevant to the nonparametric setting, where standard probabilistic inference can scale poorly and depend heavily on initialization. Results on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate advantages of the proposed framework, supporting the usefulness of the derived algorithms for discrete-state sequence modeling.
neurips-2013-small-variance-asymptotics-.tldr: Small-variance limits yield scalable, k-means-like hidden Markov model algorithms, including a version with a flexible number of states.

paragraphs: Multitask learning can share information when different tasks depend on related features. Group lasso commonly selects the same subset across tasks, but exact sharing can be restrictive. This paper considers a setting where features can be grouped by similarity and related tasks may need similar, rather than identical, features.

Sparse Overlapping Sets lasso turns that idea into a convex optimization procedure that automatically selects related features across tasks. Its motivating application is multi-subject fMRI analysis, where brain voxels serve as features for classifying functional activity. The formulation allows useful features to differ between tasks while still exploiting their organization into similar sets.

The authors derive error bounds and establish consistency for squared-error loss. Experiments on real and synthetic data show advantages over lasso and group lasso. The contribution is a less restrictive form of feature sharing with both statistical analysis and empirical support: tasks can benefit from common structure without requiring their selected features to coincide exactly.
neurips-2013-sparse-overlapping-sets-las.tldr: SOS lasso uses convex optimization to share similar features across tasks, with error guarantees and advantages in fMRI-motivated experiments.

paragraphs: Applications such as sensor placement and data subset selection can require balancing coverage or diversity against cooperative cost. This paper studies formulations where both quantities are submodular. One minimizes a submodular objective while requiring another submodular quantity to exceed a threshold; the other maximizes an objective under a submodular upper-bound constraint.

The distinction between these constrained formulations and subtracting one submodular function from another matters theoretically. The difference formulation can be inapproximable in the worst case. For the constrained problems, the authors obtain bounded approximation guarantees, providing explicit control over how the algorithmic solution relates to the optimum.

The paper also shows a close relationship between the two problems: an approximation algorithm for one can yield an approximation guarantee for the other. Hardness results establish that the approximation factors are tight up to logarithmic factors. Empirical results demonstrate performance and good scalability. Together, the results make constrained formulations useful both for expressing application requirements and for obtaining meaningful algorithmic guarantees.
neurips-2013-submodular-optimization-wit.tldr: Submodular cover and knapsack formulations yield bounded approximation guarantees, linked algorithms, and hardness results tight up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search aims to find data points close to a query. Binary space-partitioning trees organize this search by repeatedly dividing the space. The family includes kd-trees, principal-axis trees, and random-projection trees. This paper investigates which properties of these trees provide a principled basis for choosing a search structure.

The authors connect search guarantees to vector quantization performance, which concerns how well a partition-based representation summarizes the data. Their theoretical results imply that trees with better quantization performance have better search performance guarantees. This supplies a measurable structural criterion for comparing trees beyond simply choosing among named construction methods.

A second factor is the margin of the partitions: the separation associated with the tree's splits. The paper provides theoretical and empirical evidence that large-margin partitions can improve search performance. Together, the findings identify quantization quality and partition margins as useful considerations in tree design. The result offers criteria for evaluating search structures rather than declaring one tree family universally best.
neurips-2013-which-space-partitioning-tr.tldr: Better vector quantization yields stronger tree-search guarantees, while larger partition margins can improve nearest-neighbor search performance.
